title: Required attribution for pre-execution governance of AI agent payments (x402): same verdict, different culprit
description: AI agents can now pay for things on their own, over settlement rails that do not govern the payer. Several systems published in 2026 put a deterministic check in front of an agent's action. We do not propose another one. We argue that this category, which already has independent implementations, is missing one property, and we work out what it costs to require it. When controls can only make a verdict stricter, the final verdict is the strictest one any control proposed, so the order the controls run in does not change it. The record of which control decided is a different matter. The last control to tighten the verdict is the first one in the order to reach the maximum, so attribution depends on order exactly when two or more controls reach that maximum. That happens all the time: any two outright refusals tie at the top. So a specification that requires attribution has to choose: fix the evaluation order, declare which controls win a tie, or record the full set of controls that reached the verdict. The set does not depend on order, and it names exactly the controls an operator must change before a refused payment can go through; it costs running every control after the outcome is already settled. We make three contributions, each of which changes what a specification must say or what an audit can check. Attribution as a required output that a third party can score from machine-readable vectors, on approvals as well as refusals, with set-valued attribution as its order-free form. A disclosure rule we call *bounded, not eliminated*, which obliges an implementation to state what its control leaves behind. And a benchmark scoring rule, `DEFENDED_BY_ACCIDENT`, which counts an attack refused by a control that was not aiming at it as a finding rather than a pass. The paper also maps where such a control can sit on an x402 payment (a pre-tool hook, the client's spend controls, a custodial signer, an agent gateway, the seller, the facilitator) and what each position can and cannot see. A pre-tool hook decides before the seller has named a price. A gateway sees the signed amount but cannot revoke it. No position holds an independent view of what the price should have been. The reference implementation scores 17 of 20 attacks defended, one by accident and two open by design. The instrument has no benign scenarios, so an implementation that refused everything would score perfectly; we found that defect by reading a competitor's design. Three prior-art surveys removed three larger claims while we wrote this, and Section 3 reports each removal.
